subject: Cooking
title: Searing Meat Doesn't Seal in Juices
description: A 60-second lesson on Searing Meat Doesn't Seal in Juices.

hook.text: Every cooking show says it: sear meat to 'seal in the juices.' It's the biggest myth in the kitchen.

buildup.text: German chemist Justus von Liebig proposed this theory in 1850. Cooks have repeated it ever since.

discovery.text: Experiments show seared meat actually loses more moisture than meat cooked gently from the start.

twist.text: Searing is still valuable — but for flavor, not moisture. The Maillard reaction creates hundreds of tasty compounds.

climax.text: A crust doesn't seal anything. It's porous. Juices escape freely through cracks in the seared surface.

punchline.text: Sear for flavor, not for sealing. The juice myth is 170 years overdue for.

quiz.question: Why should you sear meat according to food science?

details.summary: The idea that searing meat creates a seal that locks in juices was disproven decades ago. Seared meat actually loses more moisture than gently cooked meat. Searing is still valuable — it triggers the Maillard reaction, creating hundreds of flavorful compounds on the surface.
details.whyItMatters: This persistent myth leads cooks to overcook meat chasing a nonexistent seal. Understanding that searing is about flavor, not moisture retention, improves cooking results immediately.
takeaways: Searing does not create an impermeable seal on meat surfaces
Seared meat loses more moisture than gently cooked meat
The Maillard reaction is the real reason searing tastes great

faq.question: Who proved that searing does not seal in juices?
faq.answer: Food scientist Harold McGee demonstrated this conclusively by weighing meat before and after searing versus gentle cooking. The seared meat consistently weighed less, proving it lost more moisture. The myth originated from a 19th-century German chemist's untested theory.

faq.question: Should you still sear meat before cooking?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Searing creates delicious browning through the Maillard reaction, producing complex flavors and aromas that slow cooking alone cannot achieve. Just understand the reason is flavor, not moisture. Many chefs now reverse-sear: cook gently first, then sear at the end.
